items.content:
After Democratic candidate Scott Colom met with supporters at a senior center, Democracy Docket spoke with Peggy Smith, 78, about the election’s significance to her.

She recalled protesting for school integration in 1963. Now, she says she’s “ecstatic” how far Mississippi has come.

“This is going to be a history-making decision if we come out — not if, but when — Scott comes out [on top],” she told Democracy Docket. “And it just reminds me of the years that we marched and that we fought for our state to come out on top.”

Colom said he felt “confident” and urged voters to check if their ballots remain uncounted.

“At some point we’ve got to accept reality. We’ve got to accept the will of the voters, we’ve got to follow the process, we’ve got to be patient, but at some point we just have to start the transition because the people of Mississippi — they’re going to need their junior senator to be ready to go on day one,” he said.

items.title: What Harmeet Dhillon left out of her resignation letter
items.author: 1axckhtfz27exyoh2ko4cl96s1n5gdibde0yxv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
As the Department of Justice filed a flurry of lawsuits in the final weeks before the election to derail vote counting and certification, something was off. On my daily podcasts, I repeatedly asked: Where is Harmeet Dhillon?

Dhillon was the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights and a former Republican election lawyer. She was the architect of DOJ’s failed lawsuits to gain access to state voter files. And yet, in the homestretch, she was missing from the biggest cases.

Finally, the mystery has been solved.

We now know that in early October, Dhillon told the White House she planned to leave after the election. Yesterday, she formally resigned.

Now the question is, what happened to one of Donald Trump’s staunchest promoters of disenfranchisement?

When Donald Trump prepared to take office for the second time, he made clear that he wanted the Department of Justice to serve his personal agenda. And nothing was more important to him than vindicating his discredited theory of election denialism.

This required transforming the Civil Rights Division into an attack dog that would limit voting rights rather than protect them. The person he chose to lead this effort was Dhillon.

When he nominated her in December 2024, he described her as “one of the top Election lawyers in the Country, fighting to ensure that all, and ONLY, legal votes are counted.” While Trump may have overstated her reputation slightly, there is no question that Dhillon lent an air of respectability to the election-denier cause.

A California lawyer with strong Republican Party credentials, she carried less baggage than those closely associated with Trump’s 2020 post-election debacle. For a while, Dhillon seemed perfectly positioned to succeed in the new MAGA administration.

Yet from the beginning, Dhillon ran into problems.

Her signature legal effort was obtaining complete voter data from every state. When 30 states and the District of Columbia refused, she sued them. These cases did not go well for her.

By Election Day, DOJ had lost 27 of those cases in district court and won none. It also lost the only appeals court ruling. The losses included more than a dozen defeats before Republican-appointed federal judges, nine of them appointed by Trump himself. DOJ was having scarcely more luck defending against lawsuits challenging the administration’s efforts to restrict voting by executive order.

Taken together, DOJ’s voting litigation resembled the same failed scheme Trump’s private lawyers launched after the 2020 election. As the defeats mounted, it seemed clear that something would have to change.

It seems that “something” was Dhillon.

Yesterday, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced that he had accepted her resignation. Dhillon’s letter to Trump, which lists her achievements, makes no mention of the voter roll lawsuits.

The only election-related accomplishment she cites is her deployment of election monitors. After much excitement, this too seemed to have fizzled in the end.

With Dhillon’s resignation made public, attention immediately turned to the reason for her exit.

Some suggested she might have jumped off a sinking ship of increasingly desperate, losing voting cases demanded by the White House. As I noted above, her name was conspicuously absent from the pleadings filed in California seeking to set aside 20,000 ballots, and in Alaska, where DOJ wanted to dictate certification.

The other possibility was that she was pushed out for leading a failed legal effort to achieve Trump’s election goals. Given her dismal record in court, this too seemed plausible.

Then, late in the day, CBS News reported a third possibility: that Trump demanded she be fired after watching her brief appearance on “60 Minutes” in mid-October, feeling she had not been forceful enough.

In most respects, the interview was standard fare. Dhillon toed the White House line on distrust in elections and noncitizen voting. While Trump may have wanted something more conspiratorial, she suggested that unspecified “irregularities” had marred past elections.

What I suspect landed her in trouble was this exchange:

What I’m hearing you say is that you think it’s very unlikely that a vote, a state vote, will be challenged. But people worry about that. Can you rule it out?

Well, I don’t know what is going to happen, but I can tell you that absent some shocking contingency that is unexpected, there should be no interruption in the usual course of counting and certifying the results in the states.

The problem for Dhillon is that by the time the interview aired, DOJ had already sued California to force an “interruption in the usual course of counting” ballots in that state. Indeed, DOJ was insisting that state and local officials ignore state law and set aside ballots from 20,000 people the administration had identified as potential noncitizens.

Meanwhile, DOJ was on the verge of filing an even more outrageous lawsuit that sought to block Alaska from certifying its Senate results if Trump’s preferred candidate lost.

In Trump’s orbit, it is impossible to know what really motivates hirings and firings. Dhillon, for her part, told Fox News she was not asked to resign. The truth may lie somewhere in between.

Dhillon may have been less effective than Trump wanted and more principled than he would tolerate. She may have had red lines she would not cross, in public or in private.

Either way, her legacy will be that of someone who came to DOJ to do Trump’s bidding and fell out of favor when she failed. In that, she joins a long list of others who have learned that with Trump, loyalty is a one-way street.

items.title: Why challenges to a fair count in Mississippi and Alaska will fall flat
items.author: delivery_20261105064035.48275920.3584@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
Tensions were high going into Election Day, not only because control of Congress was up for grabs but also because President Donald Trump and his administration had spent months attempting to interfere with states’ electoral processes. Lawsuits were filed, letters were sent, and threats were made, yet in the end Democratic candidates across the country notched definitive wins with margins that, in the words of Trump, were simply “too big to rig.” Even Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton—and Trump himself—was forced to concede defeat. The judiciary played a major role in tamping down frivolous legal challenges before the vote, and now Democrats, with their handsome majorities in both the House and Senate, have a mandate to fulfill. 

Consequentially, the two biggest legal challenges that consumed the days leading up to the midterms have effectively been shut down. The Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California election officials, which argued that they must set aside some 20,000 mail ballots the federal government suspected of being cast by noncitizens, was shut down by the U.S. Supreme Court on Monday. And the day before, a federal judge dismissed the DOJ’s lawsuit in Alaska, which sought to separate and preserve certain ballots cast in the state’s Senate election in the event that Republican Dan S. Sullivan lost his race. Across the country, in almost every instance of the DOJ suing states for access to their voter rolls, the federal government lost its case.

With all of that said, it’s worth looking at what the state of play is for any ongoing election challenges with a pair of major Senate races and a number of House seats yet to be called. The AFL-CIO, one of the largest national labor unions, sued the DOJ to stop it from demanding that state and local election officials separate disputed ballots and threatening prosecution if those ballots were counted. The case has been ping-ponging between judges at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, and on Election Day, the AFL-CIO asked the full court to weigh in—all 29 federal judges—and it remains to be seen where that may take this case. Over in Alaska, there was also new DOJ activity; this time, the agency sent 20 Democrats letters informing them that they may be targets of a federal investigation over donor fraud and conspiracy charges and that they should preserve certain records. Among those who received the letters was Marc Elias, a well-known elections lawyer who has represented Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, whose Alaska race has yet to be called. It’s not clear yet where this investigation will go, if anywhere, though Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Alabama, noted in her Substack: “The idea of prosecuting these people is odd since the Alaska Supreme Court has already determined that both Dan Sullivans could be on the ballot.”

These legal challenges, though significant, are not exactly to the tune of what was happening in the aftermath of the 2020 presidential election. In fact, the tone and temperature of the president and his allies have been markedly subdued since Tuesday night, with Vice President J.D. Vance putting out a surprisingly candid assessment of the Republican Party’s losses, while House Speaker Mike Johnson publicly acknowledged that the party had lost control of the House. Come Wednesday morning, Johnson also informed his staff that he does not intend to stay on as leader in the new Congress. To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, this more muted reaction is likely because there is a realization setting in that “these intellectual wars, election administration wars, are not getting them what they’re trying to achieve, either on the political side or on the strategic side.” 

Even if a worst-case scenario breaks out in which the Trump administration or Republican candidates challenge election results or processes in tight Senate races in Alaska or Mississippi, “the heavy hitters of both the Democratic and Republican parties, with respect to legal talent, will not be spread thin,” Stewart told me. “I think it will be much easier for attacks on the democratic process to be beaten back.” That is especially true when considering Democrats’ margins of victory in certain states, like Texas and Georgia, where their candidates earned double-digit wins. Even in races that were closer, Democratic candidates secured comfortable vote counts that largely fall outside margins of error. This gives way to a math problem that Republicans simply cannot solve for; Democrats have so far earned 54 seats in the Senate, a body that confirms election results, and the Trump administration does not have a meaningful enough majority of Republicans to pressure its legal shenanigans onto this time around.

“The margins last night are too big for DOJ meddling to make any sense, and it definitely won’t work,” Ankush Khardori, a former federal prosecutor, wrote. Harry Litman, a former U.S. attorney and deputy assistant attorney general, also expressed skepticism about meddling: “The most important defense/pushback/insurance policy against attempted election interference always has been a Democratic rout, which takes away the Trumpian bogus premise of a close election decided by illegal votes.” 

The bigger question now is if and how Democrats will use their congressional majorities. They will take over as chairs of the most powerful congressional committees capable of subpoenaing every single administration official, ally, or donor and deciding whether to penalize—or even possibly impeach—any of them for actions they’ve undertaken since Trump began his lawless second term.

items.title: Trump’s Alaska meltdown says it all
items.author: 1axbpx0vlef675kwd5p26396aqqssvrq070qub@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Judging by his social media post, Donald Trump agrees with me, which is why he is focused on Alaska as his last chance to keep the Democratic Senate sweep — and his humiliating defeat — from growing any larger.

Peltola holds a narrow lead, with more ballots still to be counted. What Trump continues to ignore is that those ballots will be counted and the results certified pursuant to state law. There is no legal path to reassigning votes.

In the run-up to the election, Trump directed his Department of Justice to accomplish in court what he is still demanding on social media today. DOJ lost — badly. It filed an appeal to the Ninth Circuit but has taken no steps to seek immediate review or relief.

The lawyers at DOJ no doubt understand what Trump does not: His effort to rig the Alaska Senate election failed. His assault on free and fair elections is over.

Indeed, Trump and his cronies are now likely to face a Congress eager to conduct oversight of their abuses of power, and that oversight is certain to include their attacks on democracy.

Nowhere will the administration face greater scrutiny than in the Democratic-controlled House of Representatives. While the Senate margins have garnered much of the attention, House Democrats romped from coast to coast.

Before the election, Democrats were expected to take control of the House, but with somewhere between 225 and 235 seats. Democrats have already been declared the winners in more than 250 races, and that number continues to climb.

No party has won more than 257 House seats in over three decades, a total Democrats reached in 2008. That came in a presidential election year, a historic one at that; meeting or exceeding that number in a midterm would be astounding.

All of these victories are even more impressive given the obstacles Donald Trump put in the way of voters, election officials and Democratic candidates.

He pressured big law firms to provide him with free legal services and intimidated them out of protecting voting rights. His Department of Justice launched more than 30 cases to undermine free and fair elections. He weaponized the criminal justice system against his political opponents.

Yet despite all of that, Trump and his party not only lost but were thoroughly repudiated.

There will be many theories about why Trump failed. Some will say it was the economy and affordability. Others will point to foreign wars or health care.

Yes, those issues — plus corruption and democracy — helped motivate voters and shaped their choice of candidates. But none of it would have mattered if the machinery of elections had failed.

As we celebrate the landslide repudiation of the GOP, we must remember how close we came to losing voters’ ability to elect the candidates of their choice.

In the days ahead, I believe we will celebrate Democrats gaining Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska. I expect House Democrats to surpass 257 seats.

Once those results are certified and the celebrations have ended, it will be time for us to get to work. Never again should we have to fight the federal government to protect our elections. Never again should a president be empowered by his party to destroy democracy.

This is the defining fight of our generation. As soon as my legal work in the remaining elections is done, I am ready to take it on right here at Democracy Docket. I hope you will join me.

items.title: The Extraordinary Power of an Ordinary Act
items.author: bounce_ffd21a6f-9bd8-f111-bf5b-000d3a54442e_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
As an organization with the word “democracy” in its name, yesterday felt particularly special, unrelated to the actual results. It was special because the country did the ordinary extraordinary act of voting in massive numbers, responding with affirmation of the vision of the nation’s founders as “We the People.”   

After months of warnings about ICE at the polls and National Guard troops patrolling nearby, after threats of seized ballots and real efforts to challenge ballots in advance of a singe vote, after planning to protect the election officials who make this system work, and after worrying about and planning for all that could go wrong, Americans voted quietly and with dignity. They waited in line with patience, and their individual voices produced a loud response.

The political meaning of the results will be parsed for weeks and that is where we defer to the analysis of others. We, instead, see a nonpolitical message that is simple and crucial, no matter your political leanings. We see an electorate that said no to cruelty, no to hooded and disguised federal employees aggressively patrolling their streets and harming individuals, no to deplorable and inhumane detention conditions, and no to the deportation of their long-time friends, neighbors, classmates, and workers within their communities. We see an electorate that said it was tired of the grifting, the shouting, and the retribution.

Most importantly, we see an electorate that is begging for kindness and decency. We see an electorate that waited for its moment to say clearly that it wanted – no, needed – respect for themselves and for each other. 

To us, that is how to explain results that represent America far more than a political ideology. These new government leaders will include people from all walks of life – men and women from vastly different economic backgrounds, religions, ethnicities, family configurations, ages, and personal beliefs. 

There remains much work ahead. But today is a day to feel gratitude for an election that served as a fitting end-of-year tribute to the signing of the Declaration of Independence 250 years ago. The people met the vision and for that we should all be grateful.

Thank you for your ongoing support of LDAD. Please help us protect the rule of law and the freedoms we hold dear by volunteering for our Meeting the Moment initiative and donating to our work.

Lawyers Defending American Democracy

items.title: The most dangerous days start now
items.author: 1axblm1cumu2y3nl0g0xm7ic7vu4e4cdm8576b@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
I was up late last night poring over results and dealing with last-minute legal issues. My staff told me that the paywall for my exclusive content was set to go back up today, but I insisted we keep it down until the end of the week. There is simply too much at stake.

I was a lawyer at Democratic headquarters in 1994, when Republicans gained control of the House for the first time in 40 years. I was there when Barack Obama swept into office and brought with him a 60-seat majority in the Senate and 257 seats in the House.

Yet in some respects, what we saw last night was even more dramatic.

Democrats did not just recapture both chambers. They did it by winning seats that Republicans gerrymandered last year to prevent exactly this result, and by winning in states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Those gerrymanders backfired, pushing even more seats into the Democrats’ column. Trump’s historic unpopularity hung around Republicans’ necks and lifted Democrats.

But amid all the joy and celebration, we must not forget that this election was held in the shadow of Trump’s relentless assault on voting. Over the past two years, he has issued executive orders limiting voting and tried to enact new voter suppression laws.

At the tip of the spear has been the Department of Justice. Under Attorney General Todd Blanche, it has prosecuted Trump’s political opponents. It has threatened election officials for refusing to disregard state election laws.

The DOJ has sued and sued, and lost and lost. Its record in voting and election cases is two wins and 31 losses. And it is not done.

Ballots are still being counted, and important races have yet to be called. As I have said before, the most dangerous period in any election is the days immediately after it.

That is when, in 2020, Trump began his barrage of lawsuits. It is when the Big Lie was born.

Last night, as the returns came in and the shape of the night became clear, Weijia Jiang, CBS News’ White House correspondent, posted on social media that “the president is watching returns with cabinet members, senior staff, and advisors tonight…. Trump is not planning to push officials not to certify results or declare martial law, but they will be checking for irregularities.”

That is how far we have fallen. That is how dangerous a moment we are in.

For weeks, I have warned that we are in the midst of a constitutional crisis. The fact that a network reporter felt the need to confirm that Trump will not try to block certification or declare martial law shows how close we have come to losing our democracy.

In the days ahead, I expect my law firm will be fighting to ensure that every lawful vote is counted and that Democratic candidates prevail. We will no doubt find ourselves in court against Republican lawyers and the DOJ.

These fights won’t affect control of Congress, but they will determine how much room Democrats have to maneuver in both chambers. They will also set the stage for real oversight of, and accountability for, a president who has so far operated without either.

But the fights in court will be only part of the story. Trump used his 2020 defeat to build a movement around the Big Lie of election denial. He will no doubt try to do the same now.

Democrats have an opportunity to do the opposite: to use this victory to strengthen our elections rather than tear them down. They should seize this moment to learn from Trump’s attacks on our elections and our democracy.

That starts with laying out a more ambitious agenda to limit the ability of Trump, or any president, to threaten an election the way he threatened this one.

It also requires accelerating the growth of a new pro-democracy media ecosystem to match the one the right wing has spent years building.

Democracy Docket is part of that effort, and it depends on readers like you.

In the days ahead, I will have more to say about how I can best serve this growing movement. For now, I’m going back to work.

items.title: It’s Election Day. I’m watching.
items.author: 1axbqgdmxmrnw6o6hne4ggv0y9amawx4zt0ueb@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
A few days ago, I wrote about the storm before the storm: how free and fair elections have become a full-scale war between a president seeking to undermine and those of us fighting to protect them. So far, we have battled back the storm as we have won case after case in court.

If there is a pause, an eye in the storm, it will be today.

Election Day is as close to a sacred day as a secular democracy can have. The Supreme Court has described polling places as “an island of calm in which voters can peacefully contemplate their choices.”

As a lawyer, my job on Election Day is to watch that island and make sure that the tens of millions of voters who travel to the polls today can cast their ballots. Traditionally, this has meant ensuring polls open on time, voting lines do not grow too long, and addressing any problems that occur.

But this year is very different.

The federal government has turned into a voter suppression war machine. The Department of Justice is running a vast voter suppression effort. The Department of Homeland Security is creating faulty lists and intimidating voters. Even the U.S. Postal Service tried to join the voter suppression effort.

The Republican Party and its allies are filing litigation aimed at making voting more difficult. Their Election Day plans will undoubtedly follow a similar path.

While Democratic-controlled states will do their best to facilitate voting, their GOP counterparts make casting ballots more difficult and potentially threaten to refuse to certify Democrats who prevail.

The magic of Election Day is that it is impossible to know in advance what will happen. We can read polls, but we cannot know who will win or lose. We can predict turnout, but cannot know who will show up.

This year, we have the added uncertainty of what Donald Trump will do. Whatever it is, it will not be helpful.

That’s why my eyes are keener than ever. I am watching even more closely. My law firm has worked overtime to prepare for one single day. Here is what I will be watching for.

The DOJ has been vocal about its ramped-up poll monitoring effort, which includes about 1,000 DOJ officials dispatched as poll monitors. In defense of its monitoring effort, the DOJ told a federal judge that the officers would not be acting in their law enforcement capacity. The judge was skeptical, warning the DOJ lawyers that there would be “hell to pay” if it turns out they were lying to the court.

We will find out today if the DOJ was telling the truth. If they were not, we will quickly hear reports of officers intimidating voters, acting aggressively toward poll workers, and blocking access to polling locations. Court action will follow. I hope that is not the case.

That leads to the next thing I will be watching for: whether federal law enforcement — such as ICE agents or the FBI — interferes with voting. Legally, these agents cannot be stationed at polling locations, intimidate voters or interfere with voting.

We have been worried about this for some time. The Trump administration has been banging the drum of alleged noncitizen voting; they may use this pretext to send ICE near the polls even if not directly at them.

The DOJ is 1-29 in voting and election cases — including the huge defeat they suffered yesterday in the Supreme Court. As the GOP’s loss becomes clear from exit polls, we will watch to see if DOJ goes to court again.

If the department tries to sue, my law firm is prepared to fight back. I have faith that we will beat them once again.

Donald Trump has had a circus of election deniers in his ear telling him one thing: seize the ballots and the election machines. He considered this in 2020 but did not follow through. This time there will be no one in the White House telling him no.

Should the election results go in Democrats' favor, I would not put it past Trump to launch an effort to seize ballots.

I am almost certain Trump will cry fraud if the GOP loses the midterms. He will claim Democrats cheated and promote outlandish conspiracy theories.

However, I am interested to see if Trump places any blame on the Republicans who failed to turn out voters or run competitive races. Trump will never take accountability for his own losses, and self-reflection is beyond him.

But will he place any blame on his own party, or will he just say Democrats ran another rigged election? Only time will tell.

We are now in the eye of the storm. As you read this, voters are making their way to their polling locations. Ballots are being cast.

By this evening, we will have answers to almost — if not all — of these questions. I am watching closely today, and I am sure you are watching, too.

I will check back in with you tomorrow.

items.content:
The last several days have shown once again how deeply Donald Trump hates me. In the span of 24 hours, he suggested three times that I am a criminal who should be investigated and prosecuted.

His rage clearly stems from the humiliation I continue to inflict on him and his lawyers in court.

Trump knows well that, in the aftermath of the 2020 election, I helped defeat him and his allies in more than 60 cases challenging the outcome.

In the conventional telling of that period, I led a team of highly skilled lawyers, while Trump had a ragtag team of misfits. While that is certainly true, it obscures a fundamental weakness in the way Trump and Republicans frame their election litigation: they almost always ask courts to take votes away, not to protect them.

I am not claiming that the current crop of DOJ lawyers are all-stars. Many are no better than Jenna Ellis and Sidney Powell, the Trump allies who pushed his false 2020 fraud claims and later pleaded guilty in the Georgia election case. But some are experienced litigators who have competently handled government litigation for years.

Yet they continue to show up before judges and lose at an astonishingly high rate.

Since Trump took office, his DOJ has filed 35 election-related lawsuits. It has lost 29 and won one; five are still awaiting a ruling.

In some respects, the DOJ’s 29 losses are more astounding than the 60-plus suffered by Trump’s 2020 team. After all, in 2020, Trump’s lawyers were litigating from behind and under enormous time pressure.

The DOJ, by contrast, is not trying to overcome a nearly impossible deficit. It has had nearly two years to develop a coherent litigation strategy and to bring and sequence its cases to maximize success.

Yet it has almost nothing to show for it.

Its embarrassing record isn’t limited to the cases it files. Nearly every major effort Trump has advanced to undermine elections has been blocked by the courts.

His first anti-voting executive order, which sought to require documentary proof of citizenship to register, was halted in 2025 and permanently blocked this June. His second, issued in March, directed federal agencies to compile “state citizenship lists” and ordered the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to voters on said lists. It was blocked as well.

In October, another judge ruled that the DOJ’s scheme to collect state voter rolls and run them through the SAVE database was unlawful. Most recently, courts have barred the administration from threatening California election workers with prosecution and from sending armed federal agents door to door to question voters about noncitizen voting.

Indeed, it is difficult to find any area of voting and elections where the Trump administration has consistently prevailed.

Of the cases the DOJ filed, its only victory came in North Carolina, and it comes with an asterisk. The department sued the state over a voter registration form that did not require applicants to provide a driver’s license number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. According to the DOJ, this violated federal law. Rather than fight, the Republican-controlled State Board of Elections chose to settle.

Trump is not interested in protecting voters. He wants the DOJ to file suits that make voting more difficult and subvert election results. That’s why he keeps losing. Most successful voting litigation does the opposite.

Throughout Trump’s second term, the DOJ has adopted his ethos. In nearly every case, it focuses on the rare unlawful voter while showing no regard for the rights of those whose lawful votes might be cast aside.

In Alaska, for example, the DOJ sued to delay certification of the U.S. Senate race and to force the state to segregate ballots, claiming voters might confuse Sen. Dan Sullivan with a candidate who shares his name.That remedy would necessarily compromise ballot secrecy, leaving voters vulnerable to questioning from federal agents about why they supported the candidates they chose.

In California, the DOJ sued to force election officials to set aside roughly 20,000 ballots cast by voters on a Homeland Security list of alleged noncitizens. The DOJ was callously indifferent to evidence that the list swept in U.S. citizens, including people born in the United States. Indeed, even the department’s acting deputy attorney general publicly conceded that the list could contain errors.

It is no wonder the DOJ lost both Alaska and California. But Trump wants these cases filed, and the DOJ under Attorney General Todd Blanche is simply there to file them.

For my part, I look forward to the day when the DOJ returns to its core mission of protecting voting rights. Until then, I will continue to fight against these attacks on voters in court. If history is any guide, that will earn me Trump’s enmity. That's a price I am willing to pay.

items.title: “That lawyer is me”: Why Trump’s threats won’t stop me
items.author: 1axcj8xc1zjewmopzejbfpl8mn3axv6p0mz2jn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
He will try to pressure us to back away from protecting voting rights. He will try to force us to stay silent.

Trump’s many attacks on me are well known.

In 2018, he called me the Democratic Party’s “best Election stealing lawyer.” Two years later, I helped lead the effort to defeat his attempts to overturn the 2020 election in more than 60 court cases, election contests and recounts.

In 2024, he posted an article titled “Marc Elias Is Scared ... And He Should Be” and twice posted that, if elected, he intended to investigate and prosecute “Lawyers” he saw as helping political opponents.

He has followed through. In a March 2025 speech at the Justice Department, he called me and another lawyer “radicals” trying to turn America into a “corrupt, communist, third-world country.”

About a week later, he issued a presidential memorandum targeting me and my law firm by name. By then, he had already tried to sanction my prior law firm, citing work I did there in 2016.

Earlier this year, as my firm was defeating the department in dozens of cases around the country, he called me “a terrible lawyer with a horrible track record.”

I could go on. I could list the times his allies have attacked me with lies, the civil lawsuit he filed against me that was dismissed, and his weaponization of government, including the criminal investigation by special counsel John Durham launched during his first term.

But the point is simple. As he posted in 2024, he wants me to be scared. He wants all of us to be afraid to stand up to him.

He wants us to stop speaking out. He wants us to believe that he is so powerful that there is simply no point in fighting back.

To be honest, in too many places, his strategy of fear and intimidation has worked.

Large law firms have sat idly by as Trump and his cronies violate the Constitution and make a mockery of the rule of law. Too afraid to offend Trump, they sit in their fancy offices while small law firms like mine litigate scores of cases.

Large media outlets are in full both-sides mode, with occasional obsessions reminiscent of the “but her emails” craze of 2016. They, too, are hoping to keep their access to the White House and avoid unduly offending its current occupant.

Business leaders are not just silent but complicit. They shower Trump with false praise, lavish gifts and business opportunities for his family.

With the Justice Department losing in court nearly every day, I expect further escalations from Trump and his allies.

Trump wants his Justice Department to be more brazen not only in its words but in its actions. Indeed, he complained to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi — in a now-famous September 2025 Truth Social post — that people saw her department as “all talk, no action” and that “nothing is being done.”

Election Day is Tuesday, but the fight against Trump’s attacks on democracy will continue. Trump can try to intimidate me. He can try to scare. But I have never backed down before — and I will not start now.

items.title: It won’t be over on Tuesday
items.author: 1axbudyce9lddieiyelq2dsneq4y7devwtlpz3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
“I’m tired.” You’ve heard me say it before, but it's true.

I’m tired of Trump’s attacks on democracy. His assault on the rule of law.

I’m tired of the legacy media’s false equivalency and desire to please Trump.

I’m tired of big law and business leaders doing nothing while democracy is attacked.

But I’m also just tired, and I know many of you are feeling it too.

I’ve done this work for over 30 years, and no midterm election has been this critical to the future of our country. It consumes my every waking hour.

I have always worked long hours. But lately, those hours have been even longer.

When we win one case, another one pops up. When we protect one voter, Republican operatives put 10 more at risk of losing their rights. When we win a case, the GOP appeals to the Supreme Court.

Ever since Trump entered politics, I feel like Sisyphus — endlessly rolling a boulder to the top of a steep hill, only to watch it roll back down.

It is not just the hours that have me drained. It is the emotional toll.

I am not an optimist by nature, but over the last few weeks, hope has been ever harder to find than usual.

But there is another thing about this election that is different.

Every day, my inbox fills with messages from readers like you.

I go live on YouTube almost nightly to answer your questions, but also because connecting with you directly gives me energy and hope. You tell me you’re tired too. You tell me to keep going.

“We know it won't be over on Tuesday, and I'm reassured to know you'll be there,” Dean wrote.

Kellee sent me this message on Friday morning: “Who knows if anyone will read this, but it feels good to send it. Thank you all for the work you are doing to help save our democracy. Keep the faith.”

I read it, Kellee. I read all of them.

I know you’ve been working long, hard hours, too. I see the photos you send me from protests, marching with your friends and neighbors to save democracy.

Molly shared that she was on her way to the post office with her last batch of postcards to voters before the big day. “I’m proud to support your work,” she wrote.

Just as you’ve been organizing in your communities, my law firm has spent the last year preparing for the worst-case scenarios in every district and state.

We’ve planned for every scenario we can imagine. We’ve left no stone unturned, and I can feel the momentum is moving in our direction.

But Dean is right: It won’t be over on Tuesday.

These races will be close, and Trump and his lawyers will contest every last one. My team will be in court for as long as it takes, and Democracy Docket will be covering every twist and turn.

Here’s what I’m asking of you for these final days:

First, make your plan to vote and VOTE.

Second, rally your community. Check in with the friends, family and neighbors who might need a reminder, a ride or a little encouragement.

Third, share our work. We’ve taken down our paywall through the election so that everyone can get the facts. Send our coverage to someone who needs it.

And if you can, please consider becoming a Premium member. Our members make it possible for Democracy Docket to keep covering every lawsuit and every challenge long after Tuesday.

The work we have already done gives me hope for victory on Election Day, and in the long days and nights that will come after. I rest a little easier knowing that I have a powerful, hardworking pro-democracy community by my side.

Thank you. Let’s finish this together.

items.title: Month in Review: Democracy & church-state separation
items.author: 010001a1927b2403-f6576f26-f011-466f-a19e-dfca4aeeba81-000000@amazonses.com
items.content:
I’m writing this from the road – from a tour bus, in fact – as I join some of the original Freedom Riders and their families on a get-out-the-vote journey through the South called The Ride. My role is to remind people about the important and less understood role that church-state separation plays in protecting our democratic ideals of freedom and equality for all. 

By the time you read this, we’ll have spent 10 days retracing the original 1961 Freedom Ride route from Washington, D.C., to New Orleans, visiting many historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs) and speaking especially with many students along the way. 

I was honored that the organizers invited Americans United to join The Ride, and AU was excited to become an official partner and sponsor. Personally, I have treasured being able to get to know some of the original Freedom Riders and their family members – and to hear them tell their stories. Professionally, this has been an exceptional opportunity for Americans United to reach a predominantly young, Black, Christian audience, and to explore what about our work best connects with this group. 

One helpful framework was explaining how the white Christian Nationalist agenda to destroy church-state separation is connected to so many of the attacks we’re witnessing on our democracy right now – restricting voting access, dismantling DEI programs throughout the federal government, rolling back reproductive freedom and LGBTQ+ equality, and infusing our government and public schools with one far-right version of Christianity. (You can watch a short video clip of one of my speeches

here.) 

I wish you all could have heard the inspiring call to action from AU Board member the Rev. Traci Blackmon (she and her organization Faith Out Loud were key organizers of The Ride). She offered an optimistic message about the power of each person’s voice and issued a compelling call to participate in democracy.

The Rev. Blackmon made sure I had the opportunity to speak at historic Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta about AU’s fight against the misuse of religious freedom to discriminate. I will never forget the experience of being in the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s home church and quoting him about the church not being the master or servant of the state but the conscience of the state on that hallowed ground. I posed the question, “How can the church do that if it’s merged with the state?”

“God has called men to be aggressive leaders,” Wilson says. “If they fail to follow through, then they are disobeying God.”

, Butler and producer Steven Rascón go inside the homes of Wilson’s inner circle to show how fringe fundamentalist doctrines are quietly migrating from rural church pews into the heart of American national security policies pushed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who counts Wilson as one of his spiritual advisers.

items.title: The storm before the storm
items.author: 1axbilssfnjhmm40n6u442lrkqfv6jgx7vespv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
The weekend before Election Day is usually one of my favorite times.The last campaign ads have shipped, field plans are finalized and Election Day preparations are in place. The fury of last-minute charges and countercharges subsides as candidates try to deliver a positive closing message.

A seriousness settles over the electorate as election officials make final preparations for voting and vote counting.

For a few quiet days, the fate of the election lies solely in the voters’ hands.

I normally use the time to get organized and catch up on tasks I’ve set aside. I get some sleep, knowing that Tuesday will be a long night.

It is the proverbial calm before the storm that is sure to come once the polls close and states begin the process of counting ballots and certifying results.

This year, however, has been different. The weekend before Election Day has been anything but quiet. It has been the storm before the storm.

Even with the warnings that Donald Trump would try to rig the election, and even knowing that Attorney General Todd Blanche would carry out Trump’s every whim, I did not expect it to be this bad.

Over the last few weeks, we have witnessed a daily escalation in the government’s assault on free and fair elections. In the last few days, it has reached a level never before seen in this country.

Trump’s Department of Justice is trying to force election officials to set aside, or segregate, ballots it claims are suspect, and it is threatening officials who refuse to comply. It is now using the threat of criminal investigation to intimidate political opponents and their supporters.

On Friday, the DOJ admitted that federal agencies had contacted officials in five states, California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Washington, about voters it claims are ineligible to vote in the midterms.

The DOJ also revealed that it had sent letters to election officials in all 50 states, warning that they could face prison time if they do not preserve voting records for 22 months after the election.

In Alaska, the DOJ has asked a federal judge to order election officials to segregate ballots based on which candidate a voter cast their ballot for. This is a lawsuit Donald Trump has said he ordered filed.

It asserts powers the federal government does not possess. It tramples on the right of states to run their own elections and makes a mockery of the Constitution.

Yet Trump’s loyal foot soldiers filed it, and they have been bobbing and weaving ever since to avoid a ruling on motions to dismiss their frivolous case.

Now they have loudly announced a criminal investigation in the days leading up to the election.

I am not going to bother pointing out the DOJ’s policy against this type of action. Nor will I dwell on the fact that the U.S. attorney seemed unable to articulate what the potential crime would be.

Instead, I will only ask why so few are willing to speak out about what they know is happening.

In the depths of the struggle for civil rights, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that “the greatest tragedy of this period of social transition was not the strident clamor of the bad people, but the appalling silence of the good people.”

Now, as we head into Election Day, the question is not whether good people remain. It is whether they will ever speak out.

Instead, they prefer to act like nothing is really that different. This is just another election.

Acknowledging the depth of the crisis would require large law firms to defend the rule of law instead of sitting on the sidelines. It would force corporate titans to speak out instead of cutting deals with Trump. It would make the legacy media confront how their fixation on both-sides coverage has damaged their reputation and failed their profession.

Instead, they all pretend this is a normal election when it is anything but. Better to feign ignorance than to confirm their complicity.

In the coming days, the storm will grow. Donald Trump will escalate his attacks even further. That is what he has done before.

He may disrupt voting or demand more meritless lawsuits and baseless prosecutions. He might insist that ballots be seized and election certifications set aside. He might even try to declare some sort of national emergency.

What he won’t be able to do is change people’s hearts and minds. He can try to rig the maps, suppress the vote and subvert the results, but he cannot change the fact that he and his party are deeply unpopular and that they will lose this election.

I don’t know how big the blue wave will be or how many Republicans will be washed out when this storm finally breaks.

What I am certain of is that once the election is over, we must stop the DOJ from being used as a tool of naked partisan aggression. And we must insist that more people who claim to be good speak out before the next storm arrives.

items.author: 1axblouew6p92pbpe56ydtxinvrtehldbz9oe7@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
A new batch of data on North Carolina mail ballot rejections arrived in my inbox late Monday. Mail ballots are getting flagged for rejection at a rate of nearly 6%, as of an Oct. 24 count. That’s almost 4,000 ballots so far. When ballot counting ends, the number will likely be significantly higher.

While not all ballots with problems will ultimately be thrown out, they’re in limbo and essentially null until a voter takes action to resubmit or fix errors. It’s an extra hurdle to voting that many people don’t end up surmounting. What’s more, we can now definitively tie a majority of in two of the state’s largest counties — both Democratic strongholds — to a strict new rule, imposed by Republicans at the last minute, about sealing the inner envelope.

If that wasn’t enough, the latest data revealed striking rejection rates in the double digits for some of North Carolina’s most rural counties where Black voters comprise a majority of the population. Those with lower internet access and fewer resources may have never gotten the memo that there’s an entirely new and arbitrary rule about ballot sealing. And now, it could cost them their vote.

items.title: At noon today, DOJ must reveal which states it pressured
items.author: 1axbwuejwrskfhlcmsabky17r6fy3l75ojcnab@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Among DOJ’s objections was that the request covered communications from July 1 to the present. DOJ wanted to limit it to the last 30 days. That would have hidden what the agencies did in July, August and September.

The question is why. What are they hiding? What threats have they made? What deals have they cut?

I am not naive enough to think that one court order requiring an answer to one question will end Trump’s assault on free and fair elections. I know that even after this disclosure, much of this pressure campaign will remain secret.

But it is an important step toward understanding the scope and scale of this scheme to corrupt the midterm vote count.

Interestingly, in his order, Judge Boasberg offered DOJ and DHS a way out of answering this question, and out of the entire lawsuit. “Defendants may moot this process at any time,” he wrote, “by filing a notice indicating that they will not engage in the conduct sought to be enjoined in connection with the upcoming election.”

In other words, if Trump and his cronies simply agree to stop threatening and coercing election officials and workers into not counting votes, the entire case will go away. Yet they will never accept this simple resolution.

Trump wants the threats to continue. Indeed, he wants them to escalate. And they are escalating.

According to The New York Times, DOJ has now served grand jury subpoenas on election workers in Los Angeles County, ordering them to appear with records on Nov. 4, the day after the election.

The next step could well be search warrants and threats of indictment.

We are in the midst of a constitutional crisis in which the federal government has weaponized itself against free and fair elections. It is using its vast array of tools and hiding the full extent of its actions from public view.

We will have many more fights in the days and weeks ahead. I have no illusions about how hard this will be. A weaponized federal government is a dangerous adversary.

But at noon today, at least part of that veil of secrecy will lift. We will learn which states DOJ and DHS have been pressuring in the dark, and I will share what we learn as soon as we can.

We have to stand tall and fight back.

items.title: The election chaos is about to play out in three scary phases.
items.author: delivery_20261029100502.48141097.4768@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
The midterm elections are now underway across the country and as voters decide who should hold the levers of power in Washington, all eyes are on President Donald Trump. He’s spent the last decade baselessly questioning the integrity of U.S. elections—despite plenty of evidence finding they are safe and secure—with things coming to a violent head on Jan. 6, 2021. This year, as more and more polling is suggesting Democrats will sweep Republicans, even in solidly red districts, it raises the question: Will the president accept the results of critical House and Senate races, or won’t he? “I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump ominously responded when asked this very question on Tuesday. 

Since Trump began his second term, he’s been laying the groundwork to try to nationalize U.S. elections and go after “voter fraud” through executive action and lawsuits against states, though most of these efforts have been struck down in court. Yet, the Justice Department has not given up. In fact, in recent weeks the agency filed at least two more dubious election lawsuits against California and Alaska, plus a series of cases against immigrants for alleged noncitizen voting. The legal challenges suggest the administration is planning ahead this time around, planting lawsuits that might create a foothold in the courts for the GOP to seize on if the midterms don’t end up going their way.

To Charles Stewart III, a political scientist and professor at MIT who has spent decades studying American congressional politics, elections, and political development, the current situation created by Trump is a test of America’s democracy. “Not primarily because of fundamental shortcomings in American election administration, but because political actors associated with the Administration will attempt to delegitimize or overturn its work,” he wrote in a newly published paper, “The Day After: Threats and Guardrails in the 2026 Election.”

Stewart believes that Trump’s efforts to thwart this year’s midterms should be viewed in three distinct phases: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. In practice, this looks like Trump beginning to seed baseless claims that losing Republicans can make after Election Day: mail ballots are suspect, voter rolls are contaminated with noncitizens, slow ballot counts are evidence of fraud, and any Democratic victories in close races shouldn’t be accepted. After Election Day, the lawsuits begin, harkening back to the days and weeks following Trump’s 2020 loss to Joe Biden, and finally things might culminate at the Capitol, where lawmakers could be pressured not to certify election winners.

I spoke with Stewart to understand how this framework can help us see important red flags in the hours immediately following Election Day, plus the chances that Trump incites yet another angry mob to take over the Capitol. And is there silver lining to hold on to? 

Here’s our conversation, lightly edited and condensed for clarity.

Shirin Ali: In your paper, you drill down on the president’s efforts to undermine the midterms into three flashpoints: Before Election Day, during the vote counting and certification process, and when the new Congress convenes. Can you explain what each of these are?

The ideas behind those flashpoints come from what we've seen the Trump administration working on in the second term: two executive orders, activities at the Justice Department and Homeland Security, actions that are beginning to nibble around the edges of the election administration process. Particularly before Election Day, putting pressures on mail voting, highlighted by the executive order from this past March that basically directed the U.S. Postal Service to create a new series of procedures for handling mail voting, marrying that together with directives to DHS to create these lists of citizens. 

The second flashpoint has to do with pressures on election administration, especially election administrators and the institutions themselves. There, I think the pressures go beyond even what the administration has been doing. Certainly, a lot of the activity of the administration has been focused on the possibility that if election officials don't do what the administration wants, they will not only bring civil complaints against them, but they may very well bring criminal complaints against them. Then after Election Day, that's where we're thinking about getting the final count in. We shift into the formal process of canvassing the vote, certifying it, and making sure that we've named the winners. I'm thinking broadly about a potential replay of what happened after the 2020 election, where the Trump campaign lodged a number of lawsuits in battleground states like Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. I'm still anticipating, even more now, that coming true.

The final flashpoint is what happens when the 120th Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027, particularly the House. And there the question is whether there will be efforts to bar the seating of senators or members of the House who've been elected, specifically Democrats who would be the pivotal members of the two chambers that would flip control of the chamber to the Democrats. There's another obvious parallel with 2020, when there were efforts to deny the certification of the presidential election. 

How do the Justice Department’s lawsuits against California and Alaska fit into this?

Those are kind of jumping the gun on the timeline that I had suspected, because they're really almost preempting post-election challenges and making them pre-election challenges. About a week ago I was saying, “Well, they've filed this lawsuit against California, it’s getting kind of close to the election. If there's just California, it's kind of a weak rule in terms of applying formal pressure on the states.” Then came Alaska, and this one makes me wonder what else the DOJ is going to do in the next week to bring early lawsuits against states and kind of do a shot across the bow. 

The California lawsuit is the sort of thing that we that we've long expected the Trump administration to do, and in fact in the first administration, there were rumors that they were trying to put together a national voter database and merge it with immigration records to begin to go after states for having noncitizens on the rolls. This has been a long dream of the administration and people associated with the administration, and it's taken them basically a decade in order to act on it. It doesn't look like they've done a particularly sophisticated job, both in terms of the actual job of database matching or on the legal side.

The Alaska case seems to be the most frivolous election challenge that I can imagine, and in fact it's kind of orthogonal. It's unrelated to the things I had anticipated, because the lawsuit they're bringing is the sort of lawsuit that you would expect a candidate to bring. Really, it's up to Sen. Sullivan to bring these challenges under Alaska law and then potentially to bring a contest to the U.S. Senate. I only have to believe that the Alaska case is the classic case of pleasing an audience of one; Donald Trump wanted it and he got it. There's just no way in the world this is going to go forward. It's sort of like going after James Comey or going after the members of Congress who reminded service members they didn't have to follow illegal orders. It's really performative, to please the boss, and hard to take seriously, except the degree to which it's predictive of what we're likely to see after the election: the federal government putting the thumb on the scales of candidate-oriented post-election litigation.

Next week, immediately after Election Day is over, what are you going to be watching for?

I think there will be two things. One will be legitimate, and the other will be illegitimate. The legitimate thing is that we may very well see more losing candidates contest their elections and begin taking legal actions to try to save evidence, within the normal contest laws. Some of it may very well be performative to garner support from the administration or local political actors, but those are the ill-fated sorts of things that there's a legal framework for doing. Plus there's a legal framework for judges throwing these cases out, right? And that's the way it should happen. 

What I think we need to be prepared for, and I don't think it's going to be widespread, are candidates supported by the administration going into court to attempt to impound voting machines and ballots and to remove them from where they're normally housed. Basically, a repeat of the Fulton County event a year ago where the FBI removed ballots. Those are the things I think we should anticipate, and I think that the Department of Justice may very well take matters into their own hands that are quasi-independent of the candidates themselves. For instance, the Alaska lawsuit was just something that the DOJ did because the president wanted it. That’s a disturbing thing that I think we need to be prepared for after the election because we've already seen it happen before the election. That is the DOJ just going into places they don't like and filing lawsuits.

In your paper, you wrote, “The greatest danger is not that even a few challenges will succeed; it is that a small number of delayed certifications could matter greatly if control of either chamber is in doubt.” What did you mean by that?

If you think about Jan. 6, 2021, in Congress and leading up to that, there was a whole lot of noise in the political system about whether the vice president could refuse to accept electors and whether Congress could impose their own view on what state electors they should accept, and all those sorts of things. In retrospect, traditional constitutional election lawyers had it right all along in terms of the law. The correct person was elected president, but the political ramifications of that whole episode and Jan. 6 itself were just catastrophic for American politics and certainly transformative in many ways. The law held, the right guy was elected president, but antidemocratic elements were energized and we had a riot at the Capitol.

A social movement has arisen in the country that makes millions of dollars based on stoking a view that elections in America are illegitimate. It's an extreme view, and a minority view even within the Republican Party at that level of extremity, but it's really been politically consequential over the last six years. I think we could be in an Act 2 of that, and that's what I'm getting at here. Imagine that this was a decade ago and we're coming into a Congress where the Democrats were going to take over the chamber and have about a 20-seat lead. You wouldn't have imagined anything major to come out of any contest, any seat. There might have been a couple of contests and it might have been highly politicized, but they would have been handled in the regular order.

Imagine right now if Democrats have that same margin of success. I think we have to assume there will be at least a few members of the House on the Republican side who will make a lot of hay around refusing their being seated, refusing to allow them to vote for the speaker, pressuring the clerk not to accept their certificates of election, those sorts of things. All of those would be illegitimate. The rules of the House are very clear about the clerk of the House accepting the properly given certificates of election for members of the House for the purpose of the roll-call vote at the beginning and electing the speaker. There is a very prescribed way of handling contests in the House of Representatives, and there is no legitimate, legal way for the current Congress to be the judge of those elections. 

Now, one of the things I think will stoke the political fires, though, is the investigations into any contest that any member would want to bring in the 119th Congress. There will be pressures in the current Congress for House Speaker Mike Johnson to highly politicize those investigations, use them as opportunities to shine a spotlight on California and other states that are not cooperating with the administration over noncitizens on the rolls, for instance. Or on states with high levels of mail voting. It's going to unleash this political theater in hopes of blowing up  

regular procedures that are very clear, much more clear than the Electoral Count Act was in 2020, into something that looks like a rejection of this election. And the closer it is, the higher the stakes and the higher the temperature. 

Despite having serious concerns about what the Trump administration will do in the event Republicans lose control of Congress, you’re optimistic that the 2026 midterms will be resilient enough to withstand a Trump bashing. Why?

It starts with the decentralized nature of election administration. When I've been asked about whether the Trump administration is going to be successful in overthrowing this election, I've generally responded with two words: —they've not been very good at what they've done; and there are just not enough lawyers left in the Department of Justice, or enough immigration agents, there's not enough of anything to take over the American electoral system. If it's a matter of mobilizing the federal government, there are more local election officials running elections than there's the capacity of the Trump administration to go after enough of them. That’s decentralization.

The second thing is that we continue to see evidence that the facts-based institutions of our electoral system continue to hold. That includes state and local election officials who are nothing if not careful about following the law. And there are the county boards of elections; we've seen general election boards stand by the canvassed results. There have been several states that have passed laws over the last few years reinforcing the notion that the certifications of elections at the local level are ministerial and that the proper place for conducting contests, if something is seen to be amiss, is in the court system, not in the election boards. Finally, I think we continue to see the courts holding to what the law is, holding to the precedents that have been established in the past about what do you do when someone contests the results of an election. There's established law there, and trial courts have, on the whole, held, and when they haven't, they've been admonished or overturned on appeal. It would be nice if we didn't have to say, “Well, at the end of the day, we're relying on the Alaska Supreme Court.” It would be much better if it didn't have to get that far, but we do still have a robust and independent judiciary that has been willing to stand up to nonsense.

items.title: Make no mistake about what the DOJ is doing
items.author: 1axb0hlhpcgirr5f8ame2x9omqpbfmjiqhvhlv@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
It is nearly certain to lose its frivolous case against Alaska over certification of the Senate election. And it is threatening to sue Washington State (and lose) in a copycat of the case it just lost in California.

All this losing has not deterred the administration from escalating its attacks on our elections. To the contrary, each wave of defeats encourages Trump to propose an even more authoritarian response.

It is this escalation in its war on voting that is so troubling.

At no point in any of these cases have the DOJ or the White House reexamined their stance. Neither has even entertained the possibility that what they seek to do is illegal, unconstitutional and undemocratic.

In the California ruling, the judge observed: “Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”

Instead of reflecting on these sobering words, the DOJ immediately filed an appeal.

When I shared the news of this latest decision and the subsequent appeal, several allies assured me it would be fine because my legal team would prevail. While I appreciate the confidence, a democracy that counts on the federal government losing all of its election cases will not remain a democracy for long.

It was one thing to defeat the likes of Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell in the aftermath of the 2020 election. It is quite another to pull off the same winning percentage when the Department of Justice is on the other side.

Yet that is where we are once again for the 2026 midterm elections. And those willing to stand up and fight are largely on their own.

Sadly, the legal profession, corporate leaders and legacy media have all failed us. They will risk nothing to ensure free and fair elections.

The largest law firms stand on the sidelines and look the other way as these court fights play out. Corporate leaders are silent about the attacks on our elections. The legacy media is consumed with both-sides coverage and sanctimonious self-congratulation.

The next few weeks are going to be difficult. The lies and threats will intensify.

Trump will grow more desperate. DOJ will be further weaponized against Democrats and anyone else standing in Trump’s way.

More cases will be filed. The DOJ will lose and appeal. All eyes will turn to the U.S. Supreme Court.

I am used to this rhythm. It is my job and my obligation to do my part.

But I am warning you now: this is unsustainable.

Once this election is over, we must do more to protect democracy and free and fair elections.

That means real reforms to how we protect voting rights and how we staff and run elections. The fate of our elections can no longer depend on pro-democracy forces winning every single case in court.

We cannot afford to relive this in 2028 and beyond.

items.title: The shark I’m watching most closely
items.author: 1axb2nr7dk2hqyxwmzzjlx1yw9qgeh3szdp1nn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
We are six days away from the midterms, and Donald Trump’s unprecedented attacks on free and fair elections are continuing to escalate. Many of you have asked what to watch for and what to expect next.

A colleague of mine once coined the phrase “shark closest to the boat” to help focus on the most immediate threats. It doesn’t mean it is the only concern, but it is the most immediate.

Here is my guide to the sharks closest to the boat carrying our democracy in these troubled waters:

The Department of Justice’s lawsuit blocking ballot counting in California is the shark closest to the boat. This is the shark from “Jaws,” and it threatens to sink our democracy if we don’t call up Captain Quint.

And yes, we’re going to need a bigger boat. Especially because the DOJ has already spread this playbook to Washington State, where the DOJ demanded that the state set aside ballots from more than 400 voters it claims are noncitizens. No matter where you live, your vote is not safe.

I am certainly concerned about this shark. My legal team is already running from the beaches into the water to fight back.

U.S. District Judge David Carter is expected to issue a ruling today. The DOJ will likely lose. But that will not be the end of this shark. The department will take this case to the Supreme Court, where I am certain this shark will meet its end.

This is a frivolous case, but be warned: The shark is still circling the boat.

As a reminder, Trump’s DOJ is suing to block certification of the Senate election if Democrat Mary Peltola wins. The DOJ’s argument is baseless and weak. This case never should have been filed in the first place.

But that doesn’t mean we should rest easy. Trump is invested in this case because he is determined to steal the Senate. He claims that he’s the one who gave the go-ahead for the DOJ to file.

My law firm has moved to intervene on behalf of Peltola’s campaign and the DSCC. The DOJ must respond to the motion to dismiss by tomorrow. I expect we will see the last of this shark soon enough.

The DOJ has been threatening state election officials who are simply doing their jobs. They warned election officials they could face criminal prosecution over noncitizen voting, and as we get closer to the election, those threats are only ramping up.

On behalf of the DSCC, DCCC, DGA and Nevada Democratic Party, as well as Sen. Schumer and Rep. Jeffries, my law firm sued to stop these threats. Trump and the DOJ are clearly using intimidation to dictate who can vote and how elections are run. We will not let them win.

This is a pretty big shark that should unsettle all of us. Right now, this shark is a little further off the coastline, but it’s moving fast and picking up speed. We need to keep an eye out.

There is a shark keeping a low profile on the ocean floor. That shark is red state officials colluding with the DOJ and Trump to subvert the election results in their states.

In some states, that looks like willingly handing over voter data. In others, it’s delaying mail ballots. As early voting starts, that could be welcoming federal agents at polling locations.

While this shark hides from view of the public, we need to be aware of it and keep our eyes peeled. It could make the difference between a Democratic or Republican victory.

This is the great white shark haunting our elections. We have not seen it yet, but the sea shanties worry us. This is the shark we fear the most.

If ballot seizures happen, it will be in the days following the election. The Tina Peters of the world — MAGA election clerks colluding with Trump — will mobilize and cause mayhem at the local level. Republican governors like Ron DeSantis and Greg Abbott will likely not stop them.

I worry because our attention will be divided. We will be fighting a lot of battles on a lot of different fronts. The sharks will attack before we see them.

But that does not mean we are not ready to fight back.

When the sharks attacked in 2020, I won 64 out of 65 cases. And we will win again.

The sharks may be circling, but they are no match for us.

items.author: 1axbjrc70lq48oxwe4scqeviyd6adgbti3pa6r@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
No one is happy about Tina Peters’ big segment on 60 Minutes this week.

The former GOP clerk in a 2021 voting system breach driven by election conspiracy theories was the subject of a segment on the CBS program, which focused on the great lengths Trump went to try to get her out of prison. Peters was charged with state, not federal, crimes, so he had little to do except pressure Gov. Jared Polis (D), who caved and commuted her sentence in May.

It should come as no surprise that 60 Minutes — which has been in a complete tailspin since Bari Weiss was put in charge of CBS News — totally botched the segment. Peters and her allies are pissed that it didn’t vindicate her false and deranged claims about voting machines. More importantly, voting rights advocates and election officials are rightly angry that CBS platformed a dangerous conspiracy theorist. All of this makes me wonder: Who was this for?

  • “Hummmm it appears 60 Minutes is trying to cash in on …what did they call me?” Peters , apparently mad they called her an election denier. “Stay tuned while I set the record straight on their heavy editing to distort the truth. Coming up… wait for it! Shame on you from (sic) profiteering off of my incarceration and pain.”
  • “Tina Peters continues to sow distrust in our free and fair elections,” Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) chimed in on social media. “She's guilty as sin and a disgrace to Colorado.”

Meanwhile, 60 Minutes correspondent Bill Whitaker interviewed Polis, who continued to defend his decision to pardon Peters — even after she’s shown no remorse for her actions and continues to spread dangerous anti-voting conspiracy theories.

  • “I hope that she understands that what she did was wrong,” Polis told Whitaker.
